note: A continuously refreshed coding benchmark, the working model for contamination free evaluation.
title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code

reading.body:
LiveCodeBench prevents the inflated scores that plague code evaluation by continuously refreshing its problems from real programming competitions instead of using static benchmarks.

Most LLM benchmarks are now contaminated. Models have likely seen their test problems during training, making scores unreliable measures of actual capability. LiveCodeBench solves this by pulling fresh coding problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces published after May 2023, ensuring no overlap with training data. Testing 52 models showed that older benchmarks give inflated results, meaning many evaluations of coding LLMs circulating today are not trustworthy.

The benchmark matters for AI deployment because coding tasks are central to how large language models create value. Inflated scores lead to poor purchasing decisions and false confidence in production systems. An organization cannot reliably compare models or predict real-world performance when evaluation data has contaminated the leaderboards. LiveCodeBench's continuous refresh cycle locks that contamination out going forward.

The data does not directly address compute costs, hardware requirements, or training infrastructure. It focuses on measurement accuracy rather than the resources that underpin model scaling. However, accurate evaluation is prerequisite to rational decisions about which models warrant the compute investment to scale them further.

explain_beginner: Coding benchmarks used to grade AI models are usually created once and then reused for years, which creates a problem, if a model's training data happens to include the exact test questions or extremely similar ones, that model looks like a better programmer than it actually is. Jain and coauthors built LiveCodeBench to sidestep this by continuously pulling in new programming problems from live coding contest sites, LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, dated after a known cutoff, so the questions are guaranteed to postdate a model's training data. The benchmark also expands what measuring coding ability means, beyond generating code from a description it also tests whether a model can predict what a piece of code will output, catch and fix its own mistakes, and actually execute logic correctly, not just produce plausible looking syntax. Testing 52 different language models this way, the authors found evidence that some models perform noticeably better on older, likely seen benchmark problems than on freshly collected ones, a sign those older scores were inflated. The paper stops short of naming a fix for contamination in existing benchmarks, its contribution is a live, continuously refreshed alternative.
explain_business: For a business selecting a code generation model based on public benchmark leaderboards, this paper's practical warning is that scores on long standing static benchmarks like HumanEval should be treated with real skepticism, since the underlying test problems are old enough that some models may have effectively seen them during training. LiveCodeBench offers a more trustworthy alternative for comparing models because its problem set only includes contest problems dated after public knowledge cutoffs, and because it also measures whether a model can execute and self-correct code, not just produce code that looks right, which is closer to how a coding assistant is actually used in practice. The practical action for a team evaluating coding assistants is to check whether a vendor's reported benchmark numbers come from a contamination controlled source like this one, and to weight self-repair and execution prediction performance alongside raw code generation scores, since those better predict real world debugging and iteration usefulness in a development workflow.
explain_practitioner: LiveCodeBench sources 400 problems published between May 2023 and May 2024 from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, tagging each with its release date so evaluation can be restricted to problems released after any given model's training cutoff, directly addressing benchmark contamination rather than trying to detect it after the fact. Beyond standard code generation, the benchmark evaluates three additional capabilities, self-repair, where a model must fix code that failed its own tests, code execution, predicting a program's runtime behavior, and test output prediction, predicting what a given input produces without running the code, giving a more holistic capability profile than pass or fail generation scores alone. Across 18 base and 34 instruction tuned models, 52 total, the authors report empirical evidence of contamination and overfitting to older static benchmarks such as HumanEval, models that score unusually well on older benchmarks relative to their LiveCodeBench performance are treated as a signal of prior exposure. The authors release all prompts, model completions, and an evaluation toolkit, but the comparison is necessarily a moving target, since the live problem set keeps growing and scores from different evaluation dates are not perfectly comparable.
